q: Why does proximity to the Gironde estuary benefit Medoc vineyards?
opts: It raises the acidity of the fruit
exp: A large body of water warms and cools slowly, damping extremes and lowering frost risk. The best Medoc vineyards sit close to the water for that reason.

q: Bordeaux is moderated by the Atlantic and sheltered by the Landes forest. Which climate type is this?
exp: Ocean proximity keeps the swing between seasons narrow. It also brings rain, which is why vintage variation matters so much here.

q: In most Right Bank blends, which variety dominates?
exp: Merlot ripens earlier and suits the cooler clay soils of Pomerol and Saint-Emilion, giving the plusher, rounder style of the Right Bank.

q: A blending component ripens late and brings blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannin. Which is it?
exp: Cabernet Sauvignon's thick skins give colour and tannin, and its late ripening is why it needs the Left Bank's warm, well-drained gravel.

q: One of these is not a permitted red Bordeaux variety. Which?
exp: The classic red set is Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carmenere. Syrah belongs to the Rhone and is not permitted.

q: White Bordeaux is built mainly on which pair of grapes?
exp: Sauvignon Blanc brings aroma and acidity, Semillon weight and texture. The proportions swing between crisp Entre-Deux-Mers and richer Pessac-Leognan.

q: Petit Verdot rarely exceeds a few percent of a blend. What explains that?
opts: It is prone to noble rot
It is banned above five percent
exp: Petit Verdot ripens later even than Cabernet Sauvignon and can fail in cool years. Used sparingly it adds colour, structure and a violet note.

q: Chateau Cheval Blanc is known for an unusually high proportion of which grape?
exp: Cheval Blanc's Saint-Emilion vineyard carries far more Cabernet Franc than its neighbours, which is much of what makes its style distinctive.

q: Sauternes producers prize one grape for its thin skin and affinity for noble rot. Which?
exp: Semillon's thin skin lets Botrytis take hold readily, and its waxy texture carries the sweetness. Sauvignon Blanc is blended in for acidity and lift.

q: In 1855 brokers were asked to rank Bordeaux's wines for a world exposition held in which city?
exp: Napoleon III wanted a ranking ready for the Universal Exposition in Paris. The brokers produced the list, and it has barely changed since.

q: How many tiers does the 1855 classification of reds contain?
exp: First through Fifth Growths, or premiers through cinquiemes crus. Sauternes was classified at the same time on a separate scale.

q: On what basis were the 1855 growths ranked?
opts: A blind tasting by the brokers
exp: The brokers ranked by long-standing market price, which they took as the settled verdict on quality. No tasting was involved.

q: Only one 1855 red First Growth lies outside the Medoc. Which?
exp: Haut-Brion sits in Graves, now Pessac-Leognan, and its reputation was too great to leave out of a Medoc-focused list.

q: Baron Philippe de Rothschild campaigned for half a century over his estate's rank. Which chateau was it?
exp: Mouton's elevation in 1973 is the only substantive change ever made to the red classification, and it took decades of pressure to win.

q: At its creation, the 1855 list named how many First Growths?
exp: Lafite, Latour, Margaux and Haut-Brion. Mouton's 1973 promotion took the number to five, where it stands.

q: Chateau d'Yquem holds a rank unique in the 1855 classification. What is it?
exp: Yquem alone was placed above the First Growths of Sauternes, in a tier created for it and never given to another estate.
